newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia barley firm, output headed up - Grainco.
newsitem.headline: Australia barley firm, output headed up - Grainco.

text.p: New crop Australian barley prices remain supported by fears that parts of the European crop have suffered considerable damage from dry conditions, Rob Brealey, trading manager of Queensland co-operative Grainco Ltd, said a the weekly market report.
The market was also supported by the need for further rain for a sizeable plant to take place in some of Australia's major producing regions, Victoria and South Australia.

While forecast barley production in Australia this year was estimated to increase by about eight percent to just under 3.2 million hectares, concern about lack of planting rain in the southern states remained, Brealey said.
Old crop barley also remained supported by short-term demand from Saudi Arabia and Iran, but export values were below current domestic values of around A$175.00 a tonne delivered Brisbane.
New crop values are currently being bid at A$155.00 a tonne delivered Brisbane for November/December delivery.
Export parity for Australian malting barley looks stable as European and Canadian production estimates remain on target.

Further planting rains across much of the Australian cropping area in the past week should reinforce industry forecasts that the Australian barley crop will be slightly larger than last year at 6.6 million tonnes, Brealey said.
In 1996/97 Australia produced about 6.1 million tonnes.

Domestic new crop values will open around A$185.00 a tonne delivered port, but, as with feed barley, there remains the opportunity for problems in any of the major producing areas to support values longer-term, he said.
Domestic sorghum was relatively quiet in southern Queensland last week, with little grower selling evident at current levels. Late last week some consumer and trade buying interest emerged.

As the international market continues under pressure from weaker old corn futures, Australian domestic values in southern Queensland remained unchanged, finishing last week at A$141.00 a tonne for May delivery, while the weaker export market saw central Queensland values lower at around A$120.00 port.
Last week was relatively quiet in the cottonseed market.
Rain and the weaker Australian dollar caused most traders to take a breather to evaluate market fundamentals and assess possible direction, he said.

Domestic demand, not likely to break records this year, is ticking over at a constant pace. Dairy and feed lot consumptive requirements are firm. Additional coverage for the second half of the year and into the 1998 first quarter remains open.
Crush requirement is strong as returns for oil and meal continue to be favourable, Brealey said.
Export demand was relaxed in the past week, with the Japanese and Korean markets preferring to stand back as the Yen continued to strengthen against the U.S. dollar.
In effect this had increased the purchasing power of Japanese consuming customers significantly.
While there was a possibility of further strengthening of the cross rate, Japanese traders would continue to stand aside.

Seed prices remain firm at levels around A$148.00 to A$150.00 a tonne Downs gin to the grower. In central Queensland, most grower seed has been committed with seed being offered at A$145.00 a tonne ex-gin to domestic consumers.

Following recent rains an increased pulse crop planting seems assured in northern NSW and Queensland this year. A return to rotations, improved pulse price outlook and steady cereal prices make pulses an attractive winter crop proposition.
Prices for prompt delivery chickpeas remain strong. With little stock remaining in Queensland, any parcel coming to the market is strongly sort.

The southern market has been trading in the A$360.00 a tonne to A$380.00 a tonne range, though with 100,000 tonnes of current crop likely to be shipped out to India over the coming month to six weeks, prices may well soften.

While the Indian sub-continent has a shortfall in its production of chickpeas this season, it will find it difficult to distribute such a large volume of Australian exports because of infrastructure limitations. However, once the product is taken into the market it will leave the way clear for sound prices for Australia's upcoming new crop, Brealey said.
Price indications continue at A$310.00 a tonne to A$315.00 delivered port for Queensland chickpeas and fabre beans at around A$250.00 a tonne port for new crop.

Domestic Australian oilseed values moved slightly lower over the past week, with sunflowers finishing at A$315.00 a tonne delivered Downs depots and A$322.00 a tonne delivered Newcastle for May delivery.
Central Queensland sunflower prices finished around A$267.00-A$272.00 delivered central Queensland depot for May/July. New crop soybean prices remained steady at A$425.00 a tonne delivered Brisbane.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
